topics.title: Bearings
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: describe the direction of a place from a given point using compass points. (u, s)
describe the bearing of a place from a given point. (k, s)
apply bearings in real life situations. (u, s)
choose and uses an appropriate scale to make an accurate drawing. (k, u)
differentiate between a sketch and a scale drawing. (u, v)

body.text: The four main compass points are North, East, South and West, arranged clockwise around a circle. Between them sit North-East, South-East, South-West and North-West. Direction can be described using these points — for example, a village might lie North-East of a town.

A bearing gives direction more precisely, as an angle measured clockwise from North, always written with three digits (e.g. 070°, not 70°). A bearing of 000° is due North, 090° is due East, 180° is due South, and 270° is due West.

Henry's school is 4 km from his home on a bearing of 070°. The market is 1 km from the school on a bearing of 250°. Bearings 070° and 250° differ by exactly 180°, meaning the market lies back along the same line, on the opposite side of the school from home — so the market is 4 - 1 = 3 km from Henry's home, on the same bearing of 070°.

A scale drawing represents real distances at a fixed ratio — for example, 1 cm on paper representing 1 km on the ground — and every length and angle in it is accurate, so measurements can be taken directly from the drawing. A sketch, by contrast, is a rough diagram that shows the layout but is not drawn to scale, so no measurement can be trusted from it.

To make an accurate scale drawing, choose a scale that fits the paper comfortably: a distance of 80 km at a scale of 1 cm to 10 km becomes a line 8 cm long. Too small a scale (e.g. 1 cm to 1 km for an 80 km distance) would need an 80 cm line that will not fit on an exercise book page, while too large a scale makes the drawing too small to measure accurately.
